minyue: An ancient Baiyue kingdom located in the mountainous coastal river valleys of modern Fujian province in southeastern China. Flourishing from the 4th to late 2nd century BCE, Minyue maintained fortified towns, specialized metallurgy, and maritime trade before being annexed by Emperor Wu of Han.
au-lac: An ancient proto-Vietnamese kingdom established in the Red River Delta of northern Vietnam by Thục Phán (King An Dương Vương) around 257 BCE. Centered on the monumental spiral-walled fortress of Cổ Loa, Âu Lạc was celebrated for bronze casting and sophisticated mechanical crossbow technology before being conquered by Nanyue.
qin-dynasty: The short-lived but epochal dynasty (221–206 BCE) that first unified China under Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. Standardizing writing characters, weights, measurements, currency, and axle widths, the regime connected the Great Wall and constructed the Terracotta Army through rigorous Legalist laws, collapsing rapidly in widespread rebellions following the emperor's death.
dai: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms created during the post-Qin Chu-Han Contention in 206 BCE, situated in northern Shanxi and Hebei. Ruled by Zhao Xie, the dispossessed king of Zhao, this northern frontier realm was strategically positioned against Steppe nomads before being conquered by Han general Han Xin.
jibei: One of the short-lived Eighteen Kingdoms established in 206 BCE following the fall of the Qin dynasty, covering northern Shandong around the Yellow River mouth. Ruled by Tian An, a scion of the old Qi royal house, the kingdom was quickly overrun during the chaotic wars of the Chu-Han Contention.
western-chu: The dominant hegemony established in 206 BCE by the warlord Xiang Yu after the fall of the Qin dynasty, centered at Pengcheng (modern Xuzhou). Declaring himself the Hegemon-King of Western Chu, Xiang Yu partitioned China into the Eighteen Kingdoms, waging a monumental four-year war against Liu Bang before his defeat at the Battle of Gaixia.
zhai: One of the 'Three Qins' kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE in northern Shaanxi to contain Liu Bang in the Han River basin. Ruled by Dong Yi, a surrendered Qin general, Zhai was swiftly conquered when Liu Bang launched his surprise breakout campaign across the Qinling Mountains.
chang-shan: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms established by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, covering central Hebei with its capital at Xiangguo. Governed by the insurgent general Zhang Er, the kingdom was embroiled in regional conflicts across the northern plains before Zhang Er allied with Liu Bang to establish the Han dynasty.
han-q5349053: The revived principality of Han in the central plains of modern Henan, recreated as one of the Eighteen Kingdoms in 206 BCE. Ruled briefly by Han Cheng and later Zheng Chang under Xiang Yu's overlordship, the territory was conquered by Liu Bang's advancing forces during the Chu-Han Contention.
henan: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms established by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, occupying the strategic heartland of northern Henan centered around Luoyang. Governed by Shen Yang, a former general of Zhao, the small kingdom controlled key Yellow River crossings before submitting to Liu Bang's Han army.
jiaodong: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms created in 206 BCE on the rugged Shandong Peninsula, with its capital at Jimo. Ruled by Tian Fu, the former king of Qi, Jiaodong was destabilized by internal dynastic rivalries among the Tian clan before being reunified under Qi and eventually subdued by Han.
jiujiang: A southern principality of the Eighteen Kingdoms established in 206 BCE along the Huai and Yangtze rivers in modern Anhui and Jiangxi. Ruled by the fearsome general Ying Bu, Jiujiang originally served as a vital bulwark for Xiang Yu before Ying Bu defected to Liu Bang, helping secure the Han victory.
liaodong: A northern frontier realm of the Eighteen Kingdoms created in 206 BCE, occupying the Liaodong Peninsula in southern Manchuria. Ruled by Han Guang, the displaced king of Yan, the kingdom was established to weaken northern opposition before being forcefully seized by rival general Zang Tu.
linjiang: A southern principality among the Eighteen Kingdoms founded in 206 BCE along the middle Yangtze River in modern Hubei and Hunan. Ruled by Qin rebel leader Gong Ao and his son Gong Wei from Jiangling, Linjiang remained stubbornly loyal to Xiang Yu until captured by Han forces in 202 BCE.
nanyue: An independent kingdom established in 204 BCE by the Qin general Zhao Tuo, spanning southern China and northern Vietnam (Guangdong, Guangxi, and northern Vietnam) with its capital at Panyu (modern Guangzhou). Blending Han Chinese administrative methods with indigenous Baiyue culture, Nanyue prospered through maritime trade until annexed by Emperor Wu of Han in 111 BCE.
sai: One of the 'Three Qins' kingdoms created by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE in eastern Shaanxi, centered at Yueyang. Entrusted to the surrendered Qin general Sima Xin to guard the passes against Liu Bang, Sai was rapidly overrun when Han forces launched their northern offensive.
yin: One of the Eighteen Kingdoms established by Xiang Yu in 206 BCE, situated in northern Henan and southern Hebei with its capital at Zhaoge. Governed by Sima Ang, a former Zhao general, Yin was strategically positioned along the Yellow River before surrendering to Liu Bang's forces in 205 BCE.
yong: The primary and largest of the 'Three Qins' kingdoms established in 206 BCE in the central Wei River valley of Shaanxi, centered at Feiqiu. Ruled by Zhang Han, the celebrated former commander-in-chief of the imperial Qin armies, Yong fiercely resisted Liu Bang's invasion before falling after a prolonged siege.
han-dynasty: The golden age imperial dynasty of China (202 BCE – 220 CE), founded by Liu Bang after the Chu-Han Contention. Establishing Confucianism as the state orthodoxy, the Han created a meritocratic civil service, opened the trans-Eurasian Silk Road, invented papermaking, and expanded imperial borders into Central Asia, Korea, and Vietnam.
gojoseon: The first kingdom of ancient Korea, traditionally established in the Liaoning and northwestern Korean Peninsula around the Taedong River basin. Developing a distinctive Bronze and Iron Age culture characterized by mandolin-shaped daggers and dolmen tombs, Gojoseon challenged Yan and Han China before falling to Emperor Wu of Han in 108 BCE.
korean-jin: An ancient proto-Korean confederacy that occupied the southern half of the Korean Peninsula during the 2nd and 3rd centuries BCE. Acting as an agricultural and iron-producing trade nexus between northern Korea and the Japanese archipelago, Jin was the foundational predecessor to the subsequent Samhan confederacies (Mahan, Jinhan, and Byeonhan).
byeonhan: One of the three Samhan confederacies of southern Korea, situated along the Nakdong River valley in the southeastern peninsula. Renowned across East Asia for exceptionally rich iron mines, Byeonhan exported high-quality raw iron ingots and weaponry to northern commanderies and Yayoi Japan, evolving into the Gaya confederacy.
dongye: An ancient tribal state of the Ye people located along the central eastern coast of the Korean Peninsula in modern Gangwon province. Governed by village headmen without a central monarch, Dongye was celebrated for marine agriculture, hunting, fine horse breeding, and distinctive terraced longhouses before being absorbed by Goguryeo.
jinhan: One of the Samhan confederacies of southeastern Korea, occupying the valley basins east of the Nakdong River. Composed of twelve walled town-statelets skilled in sericulture and ironworking, Jinhan integrated immigrants from northern commanderies and Gojoseon, eventually developing into the ancient kingdom of Silla.
mahan: The largest and most powerful of the three Samhan confederacies, comprising over fifty walled town-statelets across southwestern Korea (modern Gyeonggi, Chungcheong, and Jeolla). An advanced rice-farming society organized around sacred ritual precincts (sodo), Mahan was gradually united by one of its constituent member tribes to form the kingdom of Baekje.
dong-okjeo: An ancient tribal state of the Okjeo people located along the narrow coastal strip and mountain valleys of northeastern North Korea and southeastern Manchuria. Dependent on agriculture, fishing, and cloth production, Dong-okjeo lacked a unified king and was repeatedly subjected to tributary subjugation by neighboring Gojoseon, Han commanderies, and expanding Goguryeo.
goguryeo: A powerful ancient kingdom of northern Korea and southern Manchuria, traditionally founded in 37 BCE in the rugged mountain valleys of the Yalu River basin. Renowned for fierce martial culture, heavily armored cataphract cavalry, and impregnable mountain fortresses, Goguryeo expanded into a dominant regional empire, becoming one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea.
